540.title: Mothers of the believers
540.hook: the Prophet's wives are called mothers of the believers (33:6)
540.tomorrow: Men and women, side by side
540.howItsDone: Muslims call the Prophet's wives the mothers of the believers, say 'may God be pleased with her' after their names, and learn their lives from the sira and hadith.

segments.voice: Yesterday, uswah, and your line was a beautiful example. Which small sunnah did you copy, and when? Day five hundred forty.

Khadijah. 'A'isha. Hafsah. Umm Salamah. They're names you'll hear in Muslim families, called across playgrounds and written on school forms. In Muslim books, each of these women is usually followed by a short phrase of honor: may God be pleased with her. Behind each name is a woman with her own story. And the Qur'an itself gives them, together, a title that turns a household into a family for a whole community. It's in Surah Al-Ahzab.

Pickthall: "The Prophet is closer to the believers than their selves, and his wives are (as) their mothers." Ummahat al-mu'minin: the mothers of the believers. The title meant honor and respect. It also meant, as the same surah says later, that no one could marry them after the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ. Mothers to a whole community. Who were they? The biographies list the women married to him at different times. Khadijah first, a widow and a merchant, remembered by tradition as the first to believe in his message; a report in Sahih Muslim says he married no one else while she lived. Sawdah, a widow who had emigrated to Abyssinia. 'A'isha, daughter of Abu Bakr, who became a great teacher of the early community; a large share of the hadith come through her. Hafsah, daughter of 'Umar, with whom the first gathered written pages of the Qur'an were kept. Zaynab bint Khuzaymah, called the mother of the poor for her charity. Umm Salamah, whose advice at Hudaybiyyah helped calm a crisis. Zaynab bint Jahsh, known for working with her hands and giving the money away. Juwayriyah, Umm Habibah, Safiyyah and Maymunah. Many were widows. Several came from families or tribes that had been at war with the Muslims. Biographers describe some marriages as alliances, some as acts of protection, and some as matches of affection. Sunni and Shia Muslims both use the title, and both honor Khadijah deeply; they differ in how they view some of the wives' roles in the conflicts after the Prophet's death. What the verse gives is a family: every believer, it says, has these mothers.
screen: `AND HIS WIVES ARE AS THEIR MOTHERS.` · `KHADIJAH FIRST, AND ALONE FOR YEARS.` · `TEACHERS, GIVERS, ADVISERS.` · `A COMMUNITY WITH MOTHERS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: learn one of their names. Sit, and let the breath settle. Of the names you just heard, which one stayed with you? Khadijah, the first to believe. 'A'isha, the teacher. Hafsah, who kept the pages. Zaynab, mother of the poor. Umm Salamah, the adviser. Pick one. Say her name slowly. Decide to look up one more fact about her today, from a good source. Think of what she might teach someone living now. If you pray, you can ask God to be pleased with her. The bell holds the time.
Mothers of the believers. Ummahat al-mu'minin: the title Al-Ahzab gives the Prophet's wives, honored as mothers of the whole community. Today's word.

541.title: Men and women, side by side
541.hook: a verse naming believing men and women equally, ten qualities each, with one reward (33:35)
541.howItsDone: Muslims often cite 33:35 when teaching that men and women share the same spiritual duties and the same reward, and many learn its ten pairs of qualities by heart.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the mothers of the believers, and your line was mothers of the believers. Whose name did you learn, and who did you tell? Day five hundred forty-one.

A woman in Medina has been listening to the Qur'an for years. It's beautiful. It speaks to everyone. But she has noticed something, and she says it out loud. Why does it seem to address the men, and not mention us? According to a report in the Musnad of Imam Ahmad, it was Umm Salamah, one of the mothers of the believers we met yesterday, who asked. Other reports, one of them in Tirmidhi, name other women. And the answer, the reports say, came as a verse.

Pickthall begins it: "Lo! men who surrender unto Allah, and women who surrender, and men who believe and women who believe". And it keeps going, pair after pair, ten times. The Muslim men and the Muslim women. The believing men and the believing women. The devout men and women. The truthful men and women. The patient men and women. The humble men and women. The men and women who give in charity. The men and women who fast. The men and women who guard their chastity. And the men and women who remember God much. Then one ending for all of them: God has prepared for them forgiveness and a vast reward. Listen to how it sounds in Arabic: al-muslimina wal-muslimat, al-mu'minina wal-mu'minat. The masculine plural, then the feminine, again and again, like a drumbeat. Arabic grammar normally lets the masculine plural cover everyone. This verse refuses the shortcut. It names the women every single time. Notice what the ten qualities are. Not roles, not jobs. Surrender, faith, devotion, truthfulness, patience, humility, charity, fasting, chastity, remembrance. The inner life, and the practices that shape it. Each one is open to both, and each is named for both. And the reward isn't split. One forgiveness, one vast reward. Muslims discuss many questions about men's and women's roles, and scholars and communities answer them differently. This verse is one that people on many sides of those conversations quote. Because when it comes to the things it lists, faith, patience, charity, remembrance, its answer is plain. Both, equally.
screen: `MEN WHO SURRENDER, AND WOMEN.` · `TEN QUALITIES, TEN PAIRS.` · `THE GRAMMAR REFUSES THE SHORTCUT.` · `ONE FORGIVENESS, ONE REWARD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: name one quality you share with others. Sit, and let the breath settle. Go through the ten slowly: surrender, faith, devotion, truthfulness, patience, humility, charity, fasting, chastity, remembrance. Which one do you see in someone of the other sex in your life, a sister, a brother, a colleague, a parent, a friend? Picture them, and the quality, clearly. Then notice that it's one you're trying to grow too. Same quality, same road. If you pray, you can pray for that person by name. The bell holds the time.
Men and women. The verse in Al-Ahzab that names believing men and women side by side, ten qualities each, with one reward. Today's word.

542.title: Blessings on the Prophet ﷺ
542.hook: Allah and His angels send blessings on the Prophet, so do the same (33:56)
542.howItsDone: Muslims say or write sallallahu 'alayhi wa sallam after the Prophet's name, recite the Abrahamic blessing near the end of every prayer, and many count salawat on Fridays or on prayer beads.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a verse that named believing men and women side by side, quality for quality, and your line was both, equally. Which quality did you notice you share with someone? Day five hundred forty-two.

Look at any page of a Muslim book, a sermon transcript, a social media post about the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ. After his name, there's a small curl of Arabic calligraphy, or four letters in brackets, or the words peace be upon him. On this path it's come up again and again, and it can start to feel like punctuation. But it isn't a habit someone invented to be polite. It comes from one verse in the surah we've been reading this week, a verse that says who does it first, before anyone on earth.
screen: `ONE VERSE SAYS WHO DOES IT FIRST.`

segments.voice: Surah Al-Ahzab, verse fifty-six. Pickthall: "Lo! Allah and His angels shower blessings on the Prophet. O ye who believe! Ask blessings on him and salute him with a worthy salutation." Look at the order. First Allah. Then the angels. Only then the believers, asked to join something already happening. The Arabic word is salat, the same word as the daily prayer. Bukhari records an early explanation from Abu al-'Aliya: Allah's salat is His praise of the Prophet before the angels, and the angels' salat is their prayer for him. When believers send it, it's a request: O Allah, bless him. Blessings like these are called salawat, and a common form begins Allahumma salli, O Allah, send blessings. Then there's the small curl you see in print. It stands for sallallahu 'alayhi wa sallam: may Allah bless him and grant him peace. Many Muslims say it aloud or write it when his name comes up. And there's a reason many people count them. A hadith in Sahih Muslim says that whoever sends one blessing on the Prophet, Allah sends ten blessings on that person. One out, ten back. In the daily prayer itself, near the end, Muslims recite a longer salawat, often called the Abrahamic blessing, because it asks that Muhammad and his family be blessed as Ibrahim and his family were blessed. Sunni and Shia Muslims both include the Prophet's family in it; the exact wording varies by school. So the little curl is the end of a long chain: Allah, the angels, and then anyone who reads the name and stops for one breath.
screen: `ALLAH, THEN THE ANGELS, THEN THE BELIEVERS.`

segments.voice: Today's practice is ten salawat. Sit, and let your breath slow. If you're Muslim, or want to try, say the short form ten times, quietly, counting on your fingers: Allahumma salli 'ala Muhammad. O Allah, send blessings on Muhammad. If that isn't your practice, sit with the picture from the verse instead: a blessing already moving, from Allah, through the angels, and the invitation to join in. Either way, take the remaining time in silence. The bell holds the time.
Blessings on the Prophet ﷺ. Salawat: what Allah and the angels send first, and what believers ask for, one blessing out and ten returned. Today's word.
screen: `BLESSINGS ON THE PROPHET ﷺ — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: blessings on him. Today, when you see that small curl after his name, or hear peace be upon him, slow down enough to read it as a sentence. Day five hundred forty-two.

543.title: The mountains sang with Dawud
543.hook: the mountains and birds echo Dawud's praise, and iron is made soft in his hand (34:10–11)
543.howItsDone: Muslims honor Dawud as a prophet given the Zabur; beautiful Qur'an recitation is still praised by comparing it to his voice, and many Muslims glorify Allah aloud or quietly with subhanallah throughout the day.

segments.voice: Yesterday closed Surah Al-Ahzab with blessings on the Prophet ﷺ, and your line was blessings on him. Did you slow down at his name even once? Today, a new surah. Day five hundred forty-three.

Stand in a stone stairwell, or under a highway bridge, and hum one low note. The walls hum it back. Children find this out on their own, and then they do it twice. Surah thirty-four, Saba', opens its stories with a man whose praise did that on a scale no stairwell could manage. He sang, and the hills answered. The birds joined in. And the same hands that held the song could bend iron like clay. His name is Dawud, the David of the Psalms, and today the mountains sing along.

Verse ten. Allah gave Dawud a grace, and then speaks to the landscape. Pickthall: "O ye hills and birds, echo his psalms of praise!" The Arabic verb, awwibi, carries the sense of returning, coming back again and again, the way an echo does. So the hills don't just hear him; they give the praise back. Surah Sad says it too: the mountains glorified with him at nightfall and at sunrise, and the birds gathered. In the Qur'an, Dawud is given the Zabur, a scripture Muslims connect with the Psalms. And there's a hadith that shows how his voice was remembered. When the Prophet ﷺ heard his companion Abu Musa reciting the Qur'an beautifully, he told him he'd been given one of the flutes of the family of Dawud. A voice like Dawud's became a way to praise a beautiful reciter. Then verse ten turns: and We made the iron supple for him. Verse eleven tells him to make coats of mail and to measure the links well. The singer is also a smith. And another hadith adds that Dawud ate only from the work of his own hands, though he was a king. Hold those together. The same man lifts praise so beautiful the mountains join, and sits at a workbench getting the rings of armor the right size. The verse ends with an instruction to him and his family: work righteousness. Worship and work, in one pair of hands, and the world around him answering.
screen: `A FLUTE OF THE FAMILY OF DAWUD.`

segments.voice: The practice: sing or hum a praise. Sit comfortably. If you're Muslim, or want to try, quietly hum or say subhanallah, glory be to Allah, a few times, letting the sound fill your chest. If that isn't yours, hum one low note and feel where it lands in your body, then in the room. Notice the room giving a little of it back. Then let the sound stop, and sit in the quiet it leaves. The bell holds the time.
The mountains sang with Dawud. In Surah Saba', hills and birds are told to echo his praise, and the iron softens in his hands. Today's word.
screen: `THE MOUNTAINS SANG WITH DAWUD — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: the mountains sang along. Today, do one piece of ordinary work with care, the way Dawud measured his rings, and notice if anything around you answers. Day five hundred forty-three.

544.title: The staff and the termite
544.hook: Sulayman dies leaning on his staff, and only a termite eating it reveals his death to the jinn (34:14)
544.howItsDone: Muslims believe knowledge of the unseen (al-ghayb) belongs to Allah alone, and many scholars cite this verse when warning against fortune-telling and claims that jinn reveal hidden things.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the mountains sang with Dawud, and your line was the mountains sang along. Today, his son. Did any piece of work get your full care? Day five hundred forty-four.

A king stands leaning on his staff, watching his workers. They are jinn, beings of smokeless fire, building for him: high halls, statues, basins like wells. They work hard, because he's watching. Time passes. He doesn't move. They keep working. And then something tiny, something none of them noticed, finishes its own quiet job inside the wood. The staff gives way. The king falls. He had been dead the whole time. This is Sulayman, son of Dawud, and one of the Qur'an's quietest death scenes.
screen: `HE HAD BEEN DEAD THE WHOLE TIME.`

segments.voice: Surah Saba', verse fourteen. Pickthall: "nothing showed his death to them save a creeping creature of the earth which gnawed away his staff." The Arabic is dabbat al-ard, a creature of the earth. The verse doesn't name the species. Commentators understand a woodworm or termite, the kind of thing that eats a staff from the inside, and that's where today's title comes from. How long Sulayman stood there, the Qur'an doesn't say. Some commentators guess a long while; the text is silent. Then the point of the verse: when he fell, the jinn saw clearly that if they had known the unseen, they wouldn't have kept on in humiliating toil. Here's why that stings. Commentators explain that jinn were thought to know hidden things, and fortune-tellers claimed their help. And here are the jinn, working at full speed for a master who can't see them, fooled by a man leaning on a stick. The only one who knew was a small creature chewing wood. So the verse quietly takes the air out of a big claim. In the Qur'an, the unseen, al-ghayb, belongs to Allah. Not to jinn, not to kings, not to anyone with a reputation for secret knowledge. And there's a second, gentler point. Sulayman, who had armies and wind and jinn at his command, died as everyone dies, here standing up, in the middle of an ordinary day. All that power, and his death was found out by a termite. The verse doesn't mock him. It just tells the truth about how little anyone knows.
screen: `A CREATURE OF THE EARTH, EATING THE STAFF.`

segments.voice: The practice: notice how little anyone knows. Sit still. Think of the people you'll see today. Pick one, and quietly list what you actually don't know about them: what they're carrying, what they're afraid of, what happened this morning. Let the list get long. Then notice how much of your day runs on guesses. If you'd like, rest in the verse's idea: what's unseen is held by Someone, not by us. The bell holds the time.
The staff and the termite. Sulayman's death, unnoticed by the jinn, shown only by a creature of the earth eating his staff. Today's word.

segments.voice: Your line: only the termite knew. Today, when someone sounds sure about what's really going on, theirs or yours, remember the jinn working for a king who wasn't watching. Day five hundred forty-four.

545.title: The broken dam
545.hook: the people of Sheba are given two gardens, turn away, and the dam bursts (34:15–17)
545.howItsDone: Many Muslims say bismillah before drinking and alhamdulillah after, and scholars often cite the story of Sheba when teaching that gratitude (shukr) preserves blessings.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the staff and the termite, and your line was only the termite knew. Did you catch yourself guessing about someone and calling it knowing? Day five hundred forty-five.

Nobody thanks a light switch. A gift that works every day goes invisible. Surah thirty-four carries the name of a people, Saba', Sheba, whose gift was water, held back and shared out across their fields. Near Ma'rib in Yemen, old stone ruins of a dam still stand, and commentators connect them with this story. The surah tells their story in three short verses, and it isn't really about engineering at all.

Verse fifteen. There was a sign for Sheba in their homeland: two gardens, one on the right and one on the left. And the instruction that came with them is short. Pickthall: "Eat of the provision of your Lord and render thanks to Him. A fair land and an indulgent Lord!" That last line is almost a postcard. A good land, and a Lord who forgives. Everything a people could want. Verse sixteen: but they turned away. So Allah sent on them sayl al-'arim, the flood of the dam, or as some translate it, the overwhelming flood. And their two gardens were exchanged for gardens of bitter fruit, tamarisk, and a few lote trees. Verse seventeen gives the reason in one word: kafaru, they were ungrateful. Classical dictionaries connect the root, k-f-r, with covering over. Ingratitude covers a gift, like soil over a seed, until you stop seeing it. Here's what's striking. The Qur'an doesn't list a dramatic crime. The people of Sheba weren't told to do anything hard. Eat, and give thanks. That was the whole instruction, and it was the thanks they let go. Commentators connect the burst dam with the dam at Ma'rib. The Qur'an itself doesn't give a date or name the dam. It names the pattern: a gift received without gratitude starts to come apart, and what replaces it is thin and bitter. A few verses earlier, about Dawud's family, the same surah says it plainly: few of Allah's servants are thankful.

The practice: give thanks for water. If you can, pour a glass of water and hold it. Look at it. Think about where it came from: rain, a river, a reservoir, a pipe someone laid. Take a slow sip. If you pray, you can say alhamdulillah, the praise belongs to God, as many Muslims do after drinking. If not, simply notice the gift in your hand, and how rarely you see it. Then sit with the glass, and let the quiet do the rest. The bell holds the time.
The broken dam. Sheba was given two gardens and one instruction, give thanks; they turned away, and the flood came. Today's word.
Your line: gratitude keeps the garden. Today, pick one gift you've stopped seeing, a tap, a roof, a person, and say thank you for it out loud. Day five hundred forty-five.

546.title: Wings in twos and threes
546.hook: He made the angels messengers with wings, two, three and four (35:1)
546.carry: he adds to creation as he wills
546.howItsDone: Belief in angels is one of the six articles of faith in Islam; Muslims understand them as unseen beings made of light who carry out Allah's commands, known only through the Qur'an and hadith.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sheba's broken dam, and your line was gratitude keeps the garden. Which gift did you thank out loud? Today ends the week, and opens a new surah. Day five hundred forty-six.

Ask a child to draw an angel, and you'll get two wings, every time. White, feathered, one on each side, like a bird's. It's the picture from a thousand paintings and greeting cards. Surah thirty-five opens with angels too, and in its very first verse it breaks that picture open. Not two wings. Two, or three, or four. And then a line that suggests the count doesn't stop there. The surah is called Fatir, the Originator, the One who splits creation open from nothing, and it starts by refusing to let us think we've seen it all.

Verse one praises Allah, the Originator of the heavens and the earth. Then, Pickthall: "Who appointeth the angels messengers having wings two, three and four. He multiplieth in creation what He will." Notice the word messengers. In the Qur'an, angels aren't decoration. They carry things: revelation, mercy, sometimes warning. And their wings come in numbers we aren't used to. The Arabic says mathna, wa thulath, wa ruba', in twos, and threes, and fours. Then the open door: yazidu fil-khalqi ma yasha', He adds to creation whatever He wills. Many commentators read that as a hint that four isn't a limit. And a hadith gives one example. In Sahih al-Bukhari, Ibn Mas'ud reports that the Prophet ﷺ saw Jibril in his true form with six hundred wings. Six hundred. The verse and the hadith aren't giving an anatomy lesson. Muslims believe angels are real, but unseen, made of light, and that what we know of them comes only from revelation. The point is humility about our pictures. Whatever you imagine, creation is larger, and still being added to. That fits this week, actually. We met the mothers of the believers, men and women side by side, and a blessing that starts with Allah and the angels before it reaches us. Mountains singing with Dawud. A termite that knew what the jinn didn't. A dam that broke when thanks ran dry. Again and again, the world in these surahs is bigger and stranger than the picture we walked in with.

If no bird is near, picture the last one you saw. Notice how little you'd guessed about wings before you really looked. Then close your eyes and sit with the line, He adds to creation as He wills, and let it widen whatever picture you're holding. The bell holds the time.
Wings in twos and threes. The first verse of Surah Fatir: angels as messengers with two, three and four wings, and a creation Allah adds to as He wills. Today's word.
